documents.unit: Academic Senate, Council on Educational Policy
documents.title: Guidelines for Course Syllabi (Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) Policy section)
documents.summary: The Academic Senate's Council on Educational Policy syllabus guidelines require every course syllabus to carry a generative-AI policy, but state there is no campus policy and leave the content to the instructor. The AI section adds tips: tie the policy to learning tasks, explain rationale and enforcement, and point students to UCI tools such as ZotGPT.
documents.stance_why: It sets no stance itself: 'There is no general campus policy on student use of generative AI, and the content of the policy is at the discretion of the instructor.' The decision is delegated to instructors, with only a syllabus statement required.

units.why: A mandate that every syllabus carry an AI policy: 'All course syllabi must include a policy on student use of generative AI'. It binds instructors at course start, and a required syllabus statement is P09.
units.anchor: All course syllabi must include a policy on student use of generative AI

units.why: States no campus rule exists and the policy is 'at the discretion of the instructor'. That is the instructor-sets-the-rule type P04, not P85, which concerns schools or units.
units.anchor: the content of the policy is at the discretion of the instructor
units.policy: There is no general campus policy on student use of generative AI, and the content of the policy is at the discretion of the instructor.

units.why: Says the policy can be set per course or per assignment ('at the course level and/or the assignment level'); a per-course or per-assignment rule is P04.
units.anchor: Your policy should provide guidance at the course level and/or the assignment level.

units.why: Tells instructors to weigh whether AI 'might facilitate or impede student learning' for each task, tying the AI decision to learning aims (P83) rather than to a default.
units.anchor: whether using generative AI might facilitate or impede student learning in completing the tasks
units.policy: Instructors consider the tasks required in the course and/or for each assignment and whether using generative AI might facilitate or impede student learning in completing the tasks.

units.why: Because tools change, instructors should understand current capabilities 'before course delivery'. That is a duty to stay informed (P102); the clause that the policy may need updating is secondary.
units.anchor: it is important to have the most up-to-date understanding of those capabilities before course delivery
units.policy: Instructors have the most up-to-date understanding of apps' and third-party platforms' capabilities before course delivery, in case the policy needs to be commensurately updated.
units.fit_note: Also says the policy may need to be updated when platform features change.

units.why: Asks that the syllabus 'explain how and why' AI is or is not acceptable, giving students reasons for the rule; that is P66, not P09, which only requires a statement.
units.anchor: Your syllabus should explain how and why using generative AI is or is not acceptable
units.policy: Instructors' syllabi explain how and why using generative AI is or is not acceptable for the course, for each assignment, and/or for specific tasks within assignments.

units.why: Says some course tasks may allow AI and others be 'strictly forbidden', and that differentiating guides students: a per-activity rule, P04.
units.anchor: others where it is strictly forbidden
units.policy: Some cases within the course may have AI as a helpful learning tool and others where it is strictly forbidden.

units.why: Instructors who allow AI should 'encourage students to use UCI-specific AI resources, such as ZotGPT'. A university-built tool recommended across courses is P92 (institution-approved tools) rather than the single-course P17.
units.anchor: encourage students to use UCI-specific AI resources, such as
units.policy: If a course policy allows AI, instructors encourage students to use UCI-specific AI resources, such as ZotGPT and other tools built by UCI, when possible.

units.why: Instructors should 'explain what aspects of learning the policy is intended to safeguard', which gives students the rationale for the rule (P66).
units.anchor: explain what aspects of learning the policy is intended to safeguard
units.policy: Instructors explain what aspects of learning the AI policy is intended to safeguard, to bolster student understanding and adherence.

units.why: Instructors should 'explain what constitutes a violation of academic integrity'. Nearest is P36, but this only tells instructors to define misuse and does not itself classify AI misuse as misconduct.
units.anchor: explain what constitutes a violation of academic integrity
units.policy: Instructors explain what constitutes a violation of academic integrity under their AI policy.
units.fit_note: Directs instructors to define for students what counts as an integrity violation; it does not itself classify AI misuse as misconduct.

units.why: Instructors should 'Describe how the policy will be enforced in the course'. No type covers telling students the enforcement method in the syllabus; P36 and P37 classify misuse or fix penalties, which this does not.
units.anchor: Describe how the policy will be enforced in the course.
units.uncovered_note: Instructors tell students in the syllabus how the AI policy will be enforced.

documents.unit: Division of Teaching Excellence and Innovation (Office of the Vice Provost for Teaching and Learning)
documents.title: Generative AI: Is my AI policy - and the rationale - clear on the syllabus?
documents.summary: DTEI restates the Senate undergraduate rule and a Graduate Council policy (effective February 12, 2026) that graduate syllabi and program handbooks state an AI policy. It explains that the absence of a campuswide policy is intentional and asks instructors to set, communicate and consistently apply a course-specific policy.
documents.stance_why: It sets no stance: 'There is no single campuswide policy governing student use of generative AI. Instead, the content of each policy is left to the discretion of the instructor,' and calls the absence 'intentional'.

units.why: Reports the Senate rule that syllabi 'include a clear statement addressing the use of generative AI tools'; a syllabus-statement requirement (P09).
units.anchor: all undergraduate course syllabi include a clear statement addressing the use of generative AI tools
units.policy: All undergraduate course syllabi include a clear statement addressing the use of generative AI tools.

units.why: Graduate Council policy: 'All graduate course syllabi must include a policy on student use of generative AI'; P09.
units.anchor: All graduate course syllabi must include a policy on student use of generative AI

units.why: Graduate programs are 'expected to include this requirement' in handbooks. It binds programs (admin); nearest type is P09, though it adds the program handbook as a place.
units.anchor: Graduate programs are also expected to include this requirement
units.policy: Graduate programs are expected to include this requirement, along with appropriate language, in their program handbooks.
units.fit_note: Applies the AI-statement requirement to graduate program handbooks, not only to course syllabi.

units.why: 'the content of each policy is left to the discretion of the instructor': delegation to the instructor, P04.
units.anchor: the content of each policy is left to the discretion of the instructor

units.why: Gives the reason for delegating: 'instructors are best positioned to define appropriate use within their own courses'; P04.
units.anchor: instructors are best positioned to define appropriate use within their own courses
units.policy: Because the pedagogical role of generative AI varies significantly across disciplines, course levels, and learning objectives, instructors are best positioned to define appropriate use within their own courses.

units.why: Says AI use 'may be limited or prohibited to preserve specific learning outcomes or forms of assessment', tying limits to learning objectives (P83).
units.anchor: limited or prohibited to preserve specific learning outcomes or forms of assessment
units.policy: In some contexts AI use may be limited or prohibited to preserve specific learning outcomes or forms of assessment.

units.why: Notes that 'AI tools may support exploration, drafting, or problem-solving' in some contexts, a statement that some uses can be allowed. Nearest is P15 (exploring approaches), but it also names drafting and problem-solving.
units.anchor: AI tools may support exploration, drafting, or problem-solving.
units.fit_note: Also names drafting and problem-solving as supported uses in some contexts.

units.why: Instructors are expected to 'Develop a clear, course-specific policy'; this per-course rule-setting is P04.
units.anchor: Develop a clear, course-specific policy on student use of generative AI

units.why: Instructors are expected to 'Communicate that policy explicitly in the course syllabus'; P09.
units.anchor: Communicate that policy explicitly in the course syllabus

units.why: 'Ensure that expectations are transparent and consistently applied' is a duty to apply the policy consistently. No type captures it (P09 is stating, P66 is explaining).
units.anchor: Ensure that expectations are transparent and consistently applied
units.uncovered_note: Instructors apply their AI expectations transparently and consistently across students.

units.why: 'Clear guidance helps students understand not only what is permitted, but why' states the aim of giving students reasons, P66.
units.anchor: Clear guidance helps students understand not only what is permitted, but why.

units.why: 'We recognize that this is an evolving space' says the guidance is provisional, P54.
units.anchor: We recognize that this is an evolving space

units.why: Encourages instructors to 'align your course policies with your learning goals and values', so policy follows learning objectives (P83).
units.anchor: align your course policies with your learning goals and values as educators

documents.unit: Division of Teaching Excellence and Innovation
documents.title: Syllabus Policies Governing Student Use of AI (five example statements)
tiers: AI Used Only for Editing and Grammar Check
documents.summary: A DTEI-hosted document curated by Janet DiVincenzo with five public-domain example syllabus statements, ranging from AI prohibited to AI encouraged. They are templates for instructors to adapt, so the document delegates; the statements themselves carry concrete rules on citation, reflection, verification and bias.
documents.stance_why: It is a menu of templates ('five examples of syllabi verbiage that you are free to use as is or adapt', spanning 'AI use prohibited to AI use encouraged/facilitated'), so the document delegates and lists the tiers.

units.why: Introduces five examples that 'span the gamut from AI use prohibited to AI use encouraged/facilitated', i.e. named levels of AI use (P05).
units.anchor: These examples span the gamut from AI use prohibited to AI use encouraged/facilitated.

units.why: The examples are course-wide but 'can and should be adapted for specific assignments', a per-assignment rule (P04).
units.anchor: they can and should be adapted for specific assignments based on your pedagogical rationale
units.policy: The example course-wide policies can and should be adapted for specific assignments based on the instructor's pedagogical rationale.

units.why: Advises 'reminding students of your individual assignment policies' in class, assignment instructions, rubrics and announcements. Closest is P09, but it adds repeated reminders in several channels.
units.anchor: reminding students of your individual assignment policies in one or more of the following ways
units.policy: Instructors remind students of their individual assignment policies through class time, assignment instructions, assignment rubrics or Canvas announcements ('planned redundancy').
units.fit_note: Adds repeated reminders in several channels, beyond a single syllabus statement.

units.why: Recommends a Mollick and Mollick article as 'a primer for using AI in your classroom', helping faculty learn about AI (P63).
units.anchor: One of the better primers for using AI in your classroom is this article
units.policy: The document recommends a Mollick and Mollick article as one of the better primers for using AI in the classroom.

units.why: Example 1: students should 'develop core research and writing skills first before adding AI'; the reason given is skill-building, so P41.
units.anchor: develop core research and writing skills first before adding AI
units.policy: It is critical for students to develop core research and writing skills first before adding AI.

units.why: 'The danger in letting an AI platform undertake your synthesis and writing is that you will not develop these important skills': outsourcing undermines learning (P41).
units.anchor: you will not develop these important skills
units.policy: The danger in letting an AI platform undertake your synthesis and writing is that you will not develop these important skills.

units.why: 'AI bots are famous for making things up' and it is hard to know if the output is correct: P31.
units.anchor: It may be hard for you to know if the information is correct.
units.policy: Example 1: AI bots are famous for making things up, and it may be hard for students to know if the information is correct.

units.why: 'the course policy is to avoid using AI at all for your assignments' is a default ban, P01.
units.anchor: the course policy is to avoid using AI at all for your assignments

units.why: Example 2 asks students to complete work 'without using AI-generated sources to augment, think through, or write your assignments': a default ban with one exception, P01.
units.anchor: without using AI-generated sources to augment, think through, or write your assignments
units.policy: Example 2 asks students to complete their work without using AI-generated sources to augment, think through, or write their assignments.

units.why: The exception: 'welcome to use AI tools for pre-submission editing (spell-check and grammar-check)'; the permission itself is P91.
units.anchor: you are welcome to use AI tools for pre-submission editing (spell-check and grammar-check)

units.why: 'as long as you do not use them for thinking or drafting' forbids AI from producing the work; P19.
units.anchor: as long as you do not use them for thinking or drafting

units.why: If work appears AI-written, 'I will ask you to meet with me to discuss your thinking and writing process': the instructor talks with the student before escalating (P57).
units.anchor: I will ask you to meet with me to discuss your thinking and writing process
units.policy: If a student submits work that appears to have been written using AI sources, the instructor asks the student to meet to discuss their thinking and writing process.

units.why: The instructor concludes 'more likely than not' that the student did not complete the work; this is a standard of proof for a misuse finding (P69).
units.anchor: more likely than not that you did not personally complete an assignment
units.fit_note: Gives a preponderance standard for concluding a student did not do the work, rather than a rule about what evidence counts.

units.why: The instructor 'may report a violation to the campus Office of Academic Integrity & Student Conduct', a formal reporting step (P81).
units.anchor: I may report a violation to the campus Office of Academic Integrity & Student Conduct.

units.why: Example 3: 'you are welcome to use generative artificial intelligence (AI) models with acknowledgment' permits AI by default with a condition, P02.
units.anchor: you are welcome to use generative artificial intelligence (AI) models with acknowledgment

units.why: 'all large language models have a tendency to make up facts and citations and perpetuate biases' warns that output may be wrong or biased, P31.
units.anchor: tendency to make up facts and citations and perpetuate biases

units.why: 'Image generation models can occasionally come up with offensive images' names a harm of AI output, P53.
units.anchor: Image generation models can occasionally come up with offensive images.

units.why: 'You will be responsible for any inaccurate, biased, offensive, or otherwise unethical content you submit' makes students answerable for what they submit, P29.
units.anchor: responsible for any inaccurate, biased, offensive, or otherwise unethical content you submit

units.why: 'its contribution must be cited and discussed' requires disclosure with the submission, P24.
units.anchor: If you use an AI model, its contribution must be cited and discussed

units.why: The citation must say 'What AI tool did you use?' and 'What was your prompt?', i.e. tool and prompt details (P25).
units.anchor: What was your prompt?
units.policy: The cited and discussed AI contribution states what AI tool was used and what the prompt was.

units.why: The discussion also asks whether the output was revised, whether follow-ups were asked and 'What did you learn?', a reflection on use (P26).
units.anchor: Did you ask follow-up questions? Did you chat with the tool?
units.policy: The cited and discussion of AI contribution also states whether the student revised the AI output, asked follow-up questions or chatted with the tool, and what the student learned.

units.why: Example 4: 'I encourage students to use ZotGPT' for listed tasks. A named tool the instructor recommends for the course is P17 (course-specific sanctioned tool).
units.anchor: I encourage students to use ZotGPT for the following types of tasks

units.why: Lists 'Outlining content' as an encouraged use of ZotGPT, writing support (P91).
units.anchor: Outlining content
units.policy: Students are encouraged to use ZotGPT for outlining content.

units.why: Lists 'Providing background knowledge' as an encouraged use, like a tutor or reference for concepts (P12).
units.anchor: Providing background knowledge
units.policy: Students are encouraged to use ZotGPT for providing background knowledge.

units.why: Warns 'ZotGPT is often wrong—Wikipedia is a better resource for this right now': output must be treated with caution, P31.
units.anchor: ZotGPT is often wrong—Wikipedia is a better resource for this right now
units.policy: ZotGPT is often wrong, and Wikipedia is a better resource for background knowledge right now.

units.why: Lists 'Checking grammar and syntax' as an encouraged use, which is editing support (P91).
units.anchor: Checking grammar and syntax
units.policy: Students are encouraged to use ZotGPT for checking grammar and syntax.

units.why: Students who use ZotGPT 'MUST' do three things; the first is 'Cite ZotGPT', a disclosure rule (P24).
units.anchor: Cite ZotGPT

units.why: Students must 'Write a brief paragraph at the end of your work explaining how and why you used ZotGPT', a written reflection (P26).
units.anchor: Write a brief paragraph at the end of your work explaining how and why
units.policy: Students write a brief paragraph at the end of their work explaining how and why they used ZotGPT.

units.why: The paragraph must 'Include the prompts you used', which makes the prompts part of the disclosure (P25).
units.anchor: Include the prompts you used
units.policy: The paragraph includes the prompts the student used.

units.why: The paragraph must answer 'Who is the author of this work?' and explain it, making students state their ownership of the work (P29).
units.anchor: Who is the author of this work? Then explain your answer.

units.why: The instructor may require students 'to revise and resubmit all or parts of the assignment' if ZotGPT was not used appropriately, a remedial response (P68) rather than a stated penalty.
units.anchor: require you to revise and resubmit all or parts of the assignment
units.policy: The instructor reserves the right to require students to revise and resubmit all or parts of the assignment if the instructor concludes ZotGPT was not used appropriately.
units.fit_note: Revise-and-resubmit is a consequence tied to inappropriate use rather than a first-offense educative approach stated as such.

units.why: If the instructor suspects ZotGPT use and 'you have not included the required citation and reflection', a meeting follows; failing to disclose is the trigger (P28).
units.anchor: you have not included the required citation and reflection
units.policy: If the instructor suspects a student used ZotGPT and the student has not included the required citation and reflection, the student needs to meet with the instructor in person or through Zoom to talk about the assignment.
units.fit_note: Missing disclosure triggers a meeting; the text does not call it a violation.

units.why: 'This conversation will include knowledge checks for course content' checks understanding through a meeting (P34).
units.anchor: This conversation will include knowledge checks for course content.

units.why: Example 5: 'I expect you to use AI in this class', AI use is expected, P02.
units.anchor: I expect you to use AI in this class.

units.why: 'some assignments will require it' builds AI use into coursework, P79.
units.anchor: some assignments will require it.

units.why: 'Learning to use AI is an emerging skill, and I will provide basic tutorials': the course teaches AI use as a professional skill (P44).
units.anchor: Learning to use AI is an emerging skill, and I will provide basic tutorials

units.why: 'AI is vulnerable to discrimination because it can inadvertently (or intentionally) perpetuate existing biases' names bias as a harm, P53.
units.anchor: it can inadvertently (or intentionally) perpetuate existing biases
units.policy: AI is vulnerable to discrimination because it can inadvertently (or intentionally) perpetuate existing biases.

units.why: 'AI can be a valuable tool for augmenting human decision-making and critical thinking, but it is not a replacement': students keep doing the thinking (P32).
units.anchor: augmenting human decision-making and critical thinking, but it is not a replacement

units.why: 'unlike most tools you need to acknowledge using it' requires acknowledgment of AI use, P24.
units.anchor: unlike most tools you need to acknowledge using it

units.why: Students should 'explain how/what you used at the end of assignments', a disclosure statement (P24).
units.anchor: explain how/what you used at the end of assignments
units.policy: Students pay attention to information in their work produced from AI and explain how and what they used at the end of assignments.

units.why: 'My recommendation is to screen shot and save everything' (prompts, answers, where, why, how) is a recommendation to keep records, P26.
units.anchor: My recommendation is to screen shot and save everything
units.policy: The instructor recommends that students screenshot and save everything, i.e. what prompts they used, what answers were produced, where, why, and how.

units.why: 'basic attribution rules still apply' treats AI under existing citation rules, like an outside source (P45).
units.anchor: This is new territory, but basic attribution rules still apply.

units.why: 'Cite everything' requires citing AI-derived material, P24.
units.anchor: Cite everything

units.why: 'otherwise you are likely violating academic integrity policies' classifies uncited AI use as an integrity violation, P36.
units.anchor: otherwise you are likely violating academic integrity policies

units.why: 'If you provide minimum effort prompts, you will get low quality results' advises on prompting, P93.
units.anchor: You will need to refine your prompts to get better outcomes.
units.policy: Students refine their prompts to get better outcomes; minimum effort prompts give low quality results.

units.why: 'Don't trust anything the system says. Assume it is wrong' tells students to verify output, P31.
units.anchor: Assume it is wrong, unless you already know the answer
units.policy: Students do not trust anything the system says and assume it is wrong unless they already know the answer and can verify with trusted sources.

units.why: 'Use your best judgment to determine if/where/when to use these tools' leaves the decision to the student's judgment. No type fits (P04 is instructor-set), so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: Use your best judgment to determine if/where/when to use these tools.
units.uncovered_note: Students use their own judgment to decide whether, where and when to use AI tools, since they do not always make products easier or better.

notes: Coder B. Only the three included university-layer documents were coded; ICS 33 and ICS H32 course syllabi are screen=deferred in the collect file and were skipped per CODE.md. No new types proposed; UNCOVERED units: enforcement description in syllabus, consistent application of expectations, student judgment about when to use AI.
